intro: The following question is based on Text One, *The Town on the Postcard*, by Mira Castellanos, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: The Town on the Postcard
figures.text:
When people ask where I am from, I have learned to watch their faces. I say the name
   of my town, and there is a small pause, a polite tightening around the mouth, and
   then the question that always follows: 'Isn't that the place with the mine?' Yes, I
   tell them. It is the place with the mine. It is also the place with the best bread I
 5 have ever eaten, a river that turns copper-coloured at sunset, and a brass band that
   has played every Sunday for a hundred and twelve years. But nobody asks about the
   band.

   For a long time I did not mention it either. As a child, I believed what the
   postcards in the station kiosk told me: that our town was a grey smudge on the edge
10 of the map, a place you passed through on the way to somewhere better. The postcards
   showed the winding tower, the slag heaps and the long, low rows of miners' cottages
   under a heavy sky. Not one of them showed a person smiling. I used to think the
   photographer had simply been unlucky with the weather. Now I think he had already
   decided what he wanted to see.

15 When I was eleven, our school took part in an exchange with a school in the capital.
   Thirty of us travelled by coach for six hours, our faces pressed to the windows as
   the hills flattened and the motorways multiplied. The city was enormous and
   glittering, and I loved it at once. I loved the glass towers, the noise, the shops
   that sold forty kinds of tea. What I did not love was the way my host family spoke
20 to me.

   They were kind. I want to be clear about that. Mrs Adeyemi-Hart cooked a special
   dinner on my first night and gave me a toothbrush in case 'we didn't have them where
   I came from'. Her son asked whether I had ever seen a cinema. When I said that my
   uncle ran one, he looked at me as if I had told him my uncle ran a spaceship. They
25 had a picture of my town in their heads, and the picture had no room in it for
   cinemas, or toothbrushes, or me.

   I came home angry. I remember storming into the kitchen and telling my grandmother
   that the city people thought we lived in caves. She was rolling pastry at the table,
   and she did not stop. 'And what do you think of the city people?' she asked. I told
30 her they were rude, and spoilt, and that they all ignored each other on the trains.
   She laughed so hard that flour rose from her hands like smoke. 'So,' she said, 'now
   you have a postcard of them.'

   It took me years to understand what she meant. I had gone to the city expecting to
   be judged, and I had been. But I had also arrived with my own small, crumpled
35 picture of city people, and I had spent ten days collecting evidence to prove it
   right. Every unsmiling commuter went into my collection. Every friendly shopkeeper,
   every boy who offered me his seat, I quietly threw away.

   This is the trouble with a single picture of a place. It is not exactly false. Our
   town does have a mine, and the mine has scarred the hills. The city does have
40 crowded trains full of tired people staring at their phones. The postcard is true,
   as far as it goes. The danger is that it does not go very far, and that we are lazy
   enough to let it stand in for the whole.

   Last summer I went back to the kiosk at the station. The postcards are still there,
   curling slightly at the corners, the same grey tower under the same grey sky. So I
45 did something my grandmother would have approved of. I borrowed my father's camera
   and spent a week taking new pictures: the baker sliding loaves out of the oven at
   four in the morning, the band tuning up in the square, the children diving off the
   old bridge into the copper river. I had them printed and asked the kiosk owner if
   she would sell them. She looked at them for a long time. Then she cleared a whole
50 shelf.

   I am not asking you to love my town. I am asking you to notice how quickly you
   decide what a place is like, or what a person is like, from one image you did not
   even choose. Look for the second postcard. Then look for the third. You will be
   surprised how much of the world is hiding behind the first.

parts.text:
From lines 33–42, explain what the writer thinks about the way people judge places.

You may support your points with brief quotations.

rows.answer:
Accept any reasonable explanation, 1 mark per valid point, up to a maximum of 5 marks. For example:
• she admits that she held a narrow view of city people herself: ‘my own small, crumpled picture’
• she realises she was biased, looking for proof: ‘collecting evidence to prove it right’
• she ignored anything that did not fit: kind people she ‘quietly threw away’
• she thinks a single picture of a place is partly accurate: ‘It is not exactly false’
• she accepts the negative facts about her town, such as the mine that ‘has scarred the hills’
• she is fair to the city too, admitting its trains are full of tired people
• she believes the real problem is that such a picture is incomplete: ‘it does not go very far’
• she criticises people for being ‘lazy enough’ to accept one image as the whole truth

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *The Town on the Postcard*, by Mira Castellanos, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: The Town on the Postcard
figures.text:
When people ask where I am from, I have learned to watch their faces. I say the name
   of my town, and there is a small pause, a polite tightening around the mouth, and
   then the question that always follows: 'Isn't that the place with the mine?' Yes, I
   tell them. It is the place with the mine. It is also the place with the best bread I
 5 have ever eaten, a river that turns copper-coloured at sunset, and a brass band that
   has played every Sunday for a hundred and twelve years. But nobody asks about the
   band.

   For a long time I did not mention it either. As a child, I believed what the
   postcards in the station kiosk told me: that our town was a grey smudge on the edge
10 of the map, a place you passed through on the way to somewhere better. The postcards
   showed the winding tower, the slag heaps and the long, low rows of miners' cottages
   under a heavy sky. Not one of them showed a person smiling. I used to think the
   photographer had simply been unlucky with the weather. Now I think he had already
   decided what he wanted to see.

15 When I was eleven, our school took part in an exchange with a school in the capital.
   Thirty of us travelled by coach for six hours, our faces pressed to the windows as
   the hills flattened and the motorways multiplied. The city was enormous and
   glittering, and I loved it at once. I loved the glass towers, the noise, the shops
   that sold forty kinds of tea. What I did not love was the way my host family spoke
20 to me.

   They were kind. I want to be clear about that. Mrs Adeyemi-Hart cooked a special
   dinner on my first night and gave me a toothbrush in case 'we didn't have them where
   I came from'. Her son asked whether I had ever seen a cinema. When I said that my
   uncle ran one, he looked at me as if I had told him my uncle ran a spaceship. They
25 had a picture of my town in their heads, and the picture had no room in it for
   cinemas, or toothbrushes, or me.

   I came home angry. I remember storming into the kitchen and telling my grandmother
   that the city people thought we lived in caves. She was rolling pastry at the table,
   and she did not stop. 'And what do you think of the city people?' she asked. I told
30 her they were rude, and spoilt, and that they all ignored each other on the trains.
   She laughed so hard that flour rose from her hands like smoke. 'So,' she said, 'now
   you have a postcard of them.'

   It took me years to understand what she meant. I had gone to the city expecting to
   be judged, and I had been. But I had also arrived with my own small, crumpled
35 picture of city people, and I had spent ten days collecting evidence to prove it
   right. Every unsmiling commuter went into my collection. Every friendly shopkeeper,
   every boy who offered me his seat, I quietly threw away.

   This is the trouble with a single picture of a place. It is not exactly false. Our
   town does have a mine, and the mine has scarred the hills. The city does have
40 crowded trains full of tired people staring at their phones. The postcard is true,
   as far as it goes. The danger is that it does not go very far, and that we are lazy
   enough to let it stand in for the whole.

   Last summer I went back to the kiosk at the station. The postcards are still there,
   curling slightly at the corners, the same grey tower under the same grey sky. So I
45 did something my grandmother would have approved of. I borrowed my father's camera
   and spent a week taking new pictures: the baker sliding loaves out of the oven at
   four in the morning, the band tuning up in the square, the children diving off the
   old bridge into the copper river. I had them printed and asked the kiosk owner if
   she would sell them. She looked at them for a long time. Then she cleared a whole
50 shelf.

   I am not asking you to love my town. I am asking you to notice how quickly you
   decide what a place is like, or what a person is like, from one image you did not
   even choose. Look for the second postcard. Then look for the third. You will be
   surprised how much of the world is hiding behind the first.

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *After the Water*, by Tomás Reyes, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: After the Water
figures.text:
The boat smelt of diesel and wet rope. For three hours we nosed between the tops of
   trees, the engine coughing whenever the propeller caught on something hidden beneath
   the brown water. Somewhere under us, the boatman told me, was the road we would
   normally have driven along. I tried to imagine it: the tarmac, the lorries, the
 5 stalls selling roasted corn. All I could see was water, flat and sullen, stretching
   to a sky that looked as though it had been scrubbed with ash.

   I had covered floods before. I knew what to expect, or thought I did. In my bag were
   three cameras, eleven lenses and a notebook already half full of figures: the number
   of villages cut off, the number of families displaced, the tonnes of grain lost.
10 Figures are what editors ask for first. They fit neatly into a headline. They do not
   smell, or cry, or ask you for help.

   We reached Kanta just after midday. It had been a village of perhaps four hundred
   people. Now it was an island of rooftops and one concrete school building, its upper
   floor crowded with everyone who had nowhere else to go. Washing hung from the
15 windows. A goat stood on a corrugated roof, bleating at the water as if it could
   argue it away. On the steps that led down into the flood, a line of women were
   rinsing pots in the same water that had swallowed their homes.

   My job was to find the picture. I am not proud of how quickly I began to look for
   it. I moved from room to room, framing faces in my head before I had even said
20 hello: the old man with the bandaged foot, the baby asleep on a sack of rice, the
   boy staring out at the water with his chin on his knees. Each one, I calculated,
   might make a front page. I told myself this was how the world would be persuaded to
   care. Some of that was true. Some of it was simply habit.

   It was the boy who changed things. He could not have been more than ten. When he saw
25 my camera bag he stood up, wiped his hands carefully on his shorts, and offered to
   carry it. I said no, it was heavy. He insisted, quietly, the way a host insists that
   a guest takes the best chair. So I let him. He carried it from room to room behind
   me, holding it against his chest as if it were something precious, and every time I
   stopped he set it down gently on the driest patch of floor he could find.

30 At the end of the afternoon I asked the translator to find out his name. It was
   Issa. His family's house, he said, was the third roof from the left. He pointed it
   out as if he were showing me a fine view. Then he asked, very politely, whether my
   photographs would be in a newspaper, and whether the people who saw them would know
   that Kanta had a good school and a famous football team before the water came.

35 I did not know what to say. I had spent the whole day collecting pictures of what
   Kanta had lost. Not once had it occurred to me to ask what it had been. Issa did not
   want pity. He wanted the world to know that his village had been a place worth
   living in, and that it would be again. In his eyes, I realised, I was not a rescuer
   or a witness. I was a guest who had come at a bad time.

40 I took one more photograph before the boat left. It is not the picture that went on
   the front page; my editor preferred the baby on the rice sack. It shows Issa
   standing on the school steps with my camera bag still in his arms, grinning, the
   water behind him lit gold by the late sun. I keep it on my desk. When the figures
   start to pile up, as they always do, it reminds me that every one of them has a
45 name, a house that is the third roof from the left, and a football team that is
   famous, at least, in Kanta.

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *The Cliff Harvest*, by Freya Lindqvist, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: The Cliff Harvest
figures.text:
From the deck of the supply boat, Skarra looks like a loaf of dark bread that
   someone has dropped into the sea. It rises sheer on every side, three hundred metres
   of black rock streaked white with the droppings of a million birds. The noise
   reaches you long before the island does: a ceaseless, rattling clamour, like a
 5 stadium full of people all talking at once in a language you do not know.

   Forty-two people live here through the winter. In summer the population doubles, as
   families return from the mainland for the few weeks when the seabirds nest. I had
   come to see what the islanders call the cliff harvest, a tradition that is at least
   eight hundred years old. For a fortnight each year, the men and some of the women go
10 over the edge of the cliffs on ropes to collect young birds from their ledges. The
   birds are salted, smoked and stored. For centuries, they were what stood between
   Skarra and starvation.

   On the first morning, I followed Hallvard, a retired fisherman of seventy-one, up
   the steep path to the cliff top. He walked with his hands clasped behind his back,
15 as if he were strolling through a park, while I stumbled and gasped behind him. At
   the top, the wind hit us like a shove from a large, impatient animal. Below, the sea
   boiled white around the rocks. Hallvard pointed out where his father had fallen,
   sixty years earlier. He did so calmly, the way you might point out where a shop used
   to be.

20 The ropes were already in place, fixed to iron stakes that had been driven into the
   turf generations ago. A young woman named Eyrún clipped herself on, checked the knot
   twice, and stepped backwards into nothing. I lay flat on my stomach and peered over
   the edge, my fingers dug into the grass. She was swinging gently against the rock
   face, sixty metres down, using a long pole with a net on the end to scoop birds from
25 the ledges. Above and below her, thousands of adult birds wheeled and screamed.
   Every so often she pushed off from the cliff with her feet and drifted out over the
   drop, and every time she did so my stomach turned over.

   I had expected to feel uneasy, and I did. The young birds are plump, grey and
   fluffy, and they make a soft, complaining whistle as they are lifted from the nest.
30 On the mainland, where I live, people pay to watch them through telescopes. Here
   they are food. I found myself silently urging each chick to shuffle back into a
   crack where the net could not reach it, and at the same time willing Eyrún to be
   quick, to be safe, to come back up.

   That evening, in Hallvard's kitchen, I tried to explain how I felt. He listened
35 politely, pouring coffee so strong it was almost solid. Then he told me that the
   islanders take only a small proportion of the young birds each year, from the same
   ledges their grandparents used, and that the colony is larger now than it was when
   he was a boy. Scientists from the university come every spring to count the nests.
   'They count, we eat,' he said, and laughed. 'Both of us want the same thing. We want
40 the birds to come back.'

   I am still not sure what I think. It is easy, from a distance, to be sentimental
   about wild creatures. It is harder when you have eaten the islanders' bread, slept
   under their roof and watched a young woman risk her life on a rope for food that her
   family will rely on through the long, dark months when no boat can land. What I do
45 know is that I have never seen people more closely bound to a place, or more
   respectful of the creatures they share it with.

   On my last morning, the supply boat arrived early. As we pulled away, the noise of
   the colony followed us out to sea, gradually fading until it was no louder than the
   hiss of the waves. I watched the island shrink to a dark smudge on the horizon.
50 Somewhere on those cliffs, I knew, Eyrún was already clipping herself on to the rope
   again.

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *Rowing adventurer plucked from ocean as critics count the cost*, by a staff reporter, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: Rowing adventurer plucked from ocean as critics count the cost
figures.text:
A former banker who gave up his job to row single-handed across the Atlantic was
   winched to safety yesterday after his boat capsized in a storm, ending an expedition
   that one experienced sailor had already described as 'a disaster waiting for a
   date'.

 5 Marcus Thorne, 34, activated his emergency beacon at 3.40am after a wave estimated
   at twelve metres rolled his seven-metre rowing boat, Persistence, for the third time
   in an hour. The boat's self-righting mechanism failed, leaving him clinging to the
   upturned hull in water just warm enough, rescuers said, to keep him alive.

   A container ship, the Meridian Star, was diverted more than ninety miles to the
10 scene and stood by until a long-range rescue helicopter arrived shortly after dawn.
   Crew members described seeing a single orange figure waving from the hull 'like
   someone trying to hail a taxi in the middle of the ocean'.

   Speaking from his hospital bed last night, a pale but cheerful Mr Thorne said he was
   'gutted' that his attempt was over but 'incredibly grateful' to everyone involved.
15 'I knew the risks,' he said. 'I'd trained for two years. Sometimes the sea just
   decides it's not your turn.' Asked whether he would try again, he grinned. 'Ask me
   when I've stopped shaking.'

   Not everyone was in a forgiving mood. The operation is thought to have cost well
   over two hundred thousand pounds, most of which will be met from public funds. A
20 spokesperson for the coastguard confirmed that rescues at sea are never charged to
   those who are rescued. 'We go to anyone in danger,' she said. 'We do not stop to ask
   how they got there.'

   Others were less diplomatic. Retired yachtswoman Dame Celia Brandt, who has crossed
   the Atlantic eleven times, said Mr Thorne had set out too late in the season, in a
25 boat that had never been tested in heavy weather. 'Adventure is wonderful,' she
   said. 'But adventure with somebody else's chequebook is not adventure. It's an
   expensive hobby.' On social media, some users were blunter still, with one asking
   why 'a man who chose to sit in a bathtub in a hurricane' should receive help paid
   for by people struggling to heat their homes.

30 Supporters of Mr Thorne, who was raising money for a children's hospice, have hit
   back. His sister, Lauren, said he had spent months preparing and had followed every
   safety procedure. 'He's not a thrill-seeker,' she said. 'He's the most careful
   person I know. He labels his socks.' The appeal has raised more than forty thousand
   pounds, and donations rose sharply after news of the rescue broke.

35 It is not the first time the expedition has made headlines. In March, Mr Thorne's
   departure was delayed by a week when Persistence was found to be leaking in harbour,
   an incident he described at the time as 'a minor plumbing issue'. Critics now point
   to that episode as an early warning.

   Last night, the boat was still drifting somewhere in the Atlantic, upside down. Mr
40 Thorne said he hoped a passing ship might one day find it. 'There's a very good
   fruit cake in the forward locker,' he said. 'Whoever gets there first is welcome to
   it.'

From lines 13–22, explain how Marcus Thorne and the coastguard respond to the rescue.

You may support your points with brief quotations.

rows.answer:
Accept any reasonable explanation, 1 mark per valid point, up to a maximum of 5 marks. For example:
• Thorne is disappointed that his attempt has ended: ‘gutted’
• he is thankful to his rescuers: ‘incredibly grateful’
• he accepts responsibility: ‘I knew the risks’
• he stresses his preparation, having ‘trained for two years’
• he sees the accident as bad luck: ‘the sea just decides it's not your turn’
• he is still shaken but jokes about trying again
• the coastguard confirms that people are never charged for being rescued
• the coastguard's attitude is that everyone in danger deserves help: ‘We go to anyone in danger’
• the coastguard refuses to judge: ‘We do not stop to ask how they got there’
rows.notes: Do not credit material taken from outside the lines given. Reward all valid points, including ones not listed here. Quotations are optional; a quotation alone without an explanatory point is not rewarded.

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *Rowing adventurer plucked from ocean as critics count the cost*, by a staff reporter, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: Rowing adventurer plucked from ocean as critics count the cost
figures.text:
A former banker who gave up his job to row single-handed across the Atlantic was
   winched to safety yesterday after his boat capsized in a storm, ending an expedition
   that one experienced sailor had already described as 'a disaster waiting for a
   date'.

 5 Marcus Thorne, 34, activated his emergency beacon at 3.40am after a wave estimated
   at twelve metres rolled his seven-metre rowing boat, Persistence, for the third time
   in an hour. The boat's self-righting mechanism failed, leaving him clinging to the
   upturned hull in water just warm enough, rescuers said, to keep him alive.

   A container ship, the Meridian Star, was diverted more than ninety miles to the
10 scene and stood by until a long-range rescue helicopter arrived shortly after dawn.
   Crew members described seeing a single orange figure waving from the hull 'like
   someone trying to hail a taxi in the middle of the ocean'.

   Speaking from his hospital bed last night, a pale but cheerful Mr Thorne said he was
   'gutted' that his attempt was over but 'incredibly grateful' to everyone involved.
15 'I knew the risks,' he said. 'I'd trained for two years. Sometimes the sea just
   decides it's not your turn.' Asked whether he would try again, he grinned. 'Ask me
   when I've stopped shaking.'

   Not everyone was in a forgiving mood. The operation is thought to have cost well
   over two hundred thousand pounds, most of which will be met from public funds. A
20 spokesperson for the coastguard confirmed that rescues at sea are never charged to
   those who are rescued. 'We go to anyone in danger,' she said. 'We do not stop to ask
   how they got there.'

   Others were less diplomatic. Retired yachtswoman Dame Celia Brandt, who has crossed
   the Atlantic eleven times, said Mr Thorne had set out too late in the season, in a
25 boat that had never been tested in heavy weather. 'Adventure is wonderful,' she
   said. 'But adventure with somebody else's chequebook is not adventure. It's an
   expensive hobby.' On social media, some users were blunter still, with one asking
   why 'a man who chose to sit in a bathtub in a hurricane' should receive help paid
   for by people struggling to heat their homes.

30 Supporters of Mr Thorne, who was raising money for a children's hospice, have hit
   back. His sister, Lauren, said he had spent months preparing and had followed every
   safety procedure. 'He's not a thrill-seeker,' she said. 'He's the most careful
   person I know. He labels his socks.' The appeal has raised more than forty thousand
   pounds, and donations rose sharply after news of the rescue broke.

35 It is not the first time the expedition has made headlines. In March, Mr Thorne's
   departure was delayed by a week when Persistence was found to be leaking in harbour,
   an incident he described at the time as 'a minor plumbing issue'. Critics now point
   to that episode as an early warning.

   Last night, the boat was still drifting somewhere in the Atlantic, upside down. Mr
40 Thorne said he hoped a passing ship might one day find it. 'There's a very good
   fruit cake in the forward locker,' he said. 'Whoever gets there first is welcome to
   it.'

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *Below the Water Line*, by Owen Pritchard, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: Below the Water Line
figures.text:
The entrance to Pwll Du is a crack in a limestone hillside, no wider than a wardrobe
   door, half hidden by ferns. I had been through it more than forty times. I knew the
   first chamber, the long crawl that followed it and the low, wet passage that the old
   guidebooks call the Letterbox. That morning the sky was a clean, washed blue and the
 5 forecast promised nothing worse than a light shower in the afternoon. I told my
   sister where I was going, as I always did, and said I would be back for tea.

   Caves are quiet in a way that the surface never is. Two hundred metres in, the only
   sounds were my own breathing, the scrape of my helmet on the roof and the steady
   drip of water finding its way down through the rock. My lamp threw a small circle of
10 yellow light ahead of me, and beyond it the darkness was total, thick and patient. I
   have always found that darkness comforting. It asks nothing of you except attention.

   I noticed the change in the stream first. On the way in it had been a polite trickle
   running beside the path. Now it was louder, and the colour had changed from clear to
   the brown of weak tea. I stopped and watched it for a full minute. It was rising.
15 Not quickly, but steadily, licking a little higher up the pebbles with every surge.
   Somewhere above me, the light shower had arrived early, and it had not been light.

   I turned back at once. Every caver knows the rule: when the water rises, you do not
   finish the trip, you do not take one more photograph, you go. The crawl took me
   twenty minutes on the way in. On the way out it took eight, and I do not remember
20 most of it. I remember the cold soaking through my suit at the knees and elbows. I
   remember the roar building behind me like an approaching train. And I remember
   reaching the Letterbox and seeing that the gap between the water and the roof, which
   had been the height of my forearm that morning, was now no wider than my hand.

   There is a particular kind of fear that arrives very calmly. I knelt in the water
25 and made myself think. Behind me, the passage was filling. Ahead, the Letterbox was
   perhaps four metres long. If I went through on my back, with my face turned up to
   the roof, I could keep my mouth in the air pocket for most of the way. If the pocket
   closed while I was halfway, I would be holding my breath in the dark with no way of
   turning round.

30 I took three slow breaths, the way I had been taught, and pushed myself in. The
   water closed over my ears and the roar became a dull, enormous hum. I could feel the
   rock pressing against the tip of my nose. I moved by inches, pulling with my
   fingertips on the ceiling, counting each pull out loud into the tiny space of air.
   Seven. Eight. Nine. At eleven my helmet jammed against something and for one long,
35 airless second I could not move at all.

   Then it came free, and the roof lifted, and I was lying in a pool on the far side,
   coughing and laughing at the same time. I do not know why I laughed. Perhaps it was
   the sheer surprise of still being alive. I crawled the last hundred metres to the
   entrance and came out into a grey, hammering downpour, the ferns bent flat and the
40 hillside streaming with water. It was the most beautiful weather I had ever seen.

   I went back to Pwll Du the following summer, in a long dry spell, with two friends
   and a great deal more respect. At the Letterbox I stopped and put my hand flat
   against the roof, where my fingertips had pulled me through. It felt like nothing at
   all: cool, damp, ordinary stone. The cave had not been trying to kill me. It had
45 simply been doing what water and rock have done for a million years, and I had
   happened to be in the way.

parts.text:
Look again at lines 12–23.

In your own words, describe what happens when the writer realises the cave is flooding.

rows.answer:
Accept any reasonable points in the candidate's own words, where possible, 1 mark per valid point, up to a maximum of 4 marks. For example:
• he notices that the stream has become noisier
• the water has turned muddy brown
• he watches it carefully and sees that it is rising steadily
• he realises that heavy rain has fallen earlier than forecast
• he immediately starts to leave, following the cavers' safety rule
• he moves through the crawl much faster than on the way in
• he is soaked and cold and hears the water roaring behind him
• he reaches the low passage and finds the air gap has almost disappeared

parts.text:
Look again at lines 30–40.

In your own words, describe how the writer gets through the Letterbox and out of the cave.

rows.answer:
Accept any reasonable points in the candidate's own words, where possible, 1 mark per valid point, up to a maximum of 4 marks. For example:
• he calms himself with slow breaths before going in
• he lies on his back so that his face is close to the roof
• his ears are under water and the sound becomes a low hum
• his nose is touching the rock above him
• he pulls himself along the ceiling with his fingertips, counting aloud
• his helmet gets stuck and for a moment he cannot move
• he frees himself and reaches the pool on the other side
• he coughs and laughs with relief
• he crawls out of the cave into heavy rain

   first chamber, the long crawl that followed it and the low, wet passage that the old
   guidebooks call the Letterbox. That morning the sky was a clean, washed blue and the
 5 forecast promised nothing worse than a light shower in the afternoon. I told my
   sister where I was going, as I always did, and said I would be back for tea.

   sounds were my own breathing, the scrape of my helmet on the roof and the steady
   drip of water finding its way down through the rock. My lamp threw a small circle of
10 yellow light ahead of me, and beyond it the darkness was total, thick and patient. I
   have always found that darkness comforting. It asks nothing of you except attention.

   I noticed the change in the stream first. On the way in it had been a polite trickle
   running beside the path. Now it was louder, and the colour had changed from clear to
   the brown of weak tea. I stopped and watched it for a full minute. It was rising.
15 Not quickly, but steadily, licking a little higher up the pebbles with every surge.
   Somewhere above me, the light shower had arrived early, and it had not been light.

   I turned back at once. Every caver knows the rule: when the water rises, you do not
   finish the trip, you do not take one more photograph, you go. The crawl took me
   twenty minutes on the way in. On the way out it took eight, and I do not remember
20 most of it. I remember the cold soaking through my suit at the knees and elbows. I
   remember the roar building behind me like an approaching train. And I remember
   reaching the Letterbox and seeing that the gap between the water and the roof, which
   had been the height of my forearm that morning, was now no wider than my hand.

25 and made myself think. Behind me, the passage was filling. Ahead, the Letterbox was
   perhaps four metres long. If I went through on my back, with my face turned up to
   the roof, I could keep my mouth in the air pocket for most of the way. If the pocket
   closed while I was halfway, I would be holding my breath in the dark with no way of
   turning round.

   water closed over my ears and the roar became a dull, enormous hum. I could feel the
   rock pressing against the tip of my nose. I moved by inches, pulling with my
   fingertips on the ceiling, counting each pull out loud into the tiny space of air.
   Seven. Eight. Nine. At eleven my helmet jammed against something and for one long,
35 airless second I could not move at all.

   coughing and laughing at the same time. I do not know why I laughed. Perhaps it was
   the sheer surprise of still being alive. I crawled the last hundred metres to the
   entrance and came out into a grey, hammering downpour, the ferns bent flat and the
40 hillside streaming with water. It was the most beautiful weather I had ever seen.

   and a great deal more respect. At the Letterbox I stopped and put my hand flat
   against the roof, where my fingertips had pulled me through. It felt like nothing at
   all: cool, damp, ordinary stone. The cave had not been trying to kill me. It had
45 simply been doing what water and rock have done for a million years, and I had
   happened to be in the way.

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *The Voice on the Radio*, by Priya Lal, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: The Voice on the Radio
figures.text:
Every weekday at six o'clock, about half a million people wake up to Danny Okoro's
   voice. It is warm, quick and full of jokes, the kind of voice that makes you feel
   the day might not be so bad after all. What most of his listeners do not know is
   that, until he was nineteen, Danny could not say his own name without getting stuck.

 5 'D was the worst,' he tells me, stirring three sugars into his coffee in a café near
   the studio. 'Which is unlucky, when your name is Danny. I used to introduce myself
   as Dan-Dan-Dan until people just started calling me that. Some of them meant it
   kindly. Most of them didn't.'

   School, he says, was a daily battle. He would count the pupils ahead of him when the
10 teacher took the register, rehearsing the word 'here' over and over in his head
   until his turn came, and then it would refuse to come out. He learned to swap
   difficult words for easier ones, so that his sentences became strange and
   roundabout. One teacher wrote on his report that he was 'bright but lazy in oral
   work'. Another made him read aloud in front of the class 'to build his confidence'.
15 He describes that lesson as the longest twenty minutes of his life.

   'I wasn't angry with them,' he says now. 'They didn't understand it. Nobody did
   then. They thought if I just tried harder, or relaxed, or breathed properly, it
   would go away. That's like telling someone with a broken leg to walk more
   confidently.'

20 The turning point came in an unlikely place: a hospital radio station, where his
   older cousin volunteered. Danny went along one evening to help carry boxes and ended
   up being handed a microphone when a presenter failed to turn up. 'I was terrified,'
   he says. 'But there was something about it. Nobody could see me. Nobody was looking
   at my face waiting for me to finish. It was just me and the music and these patients
25 lying in bed who were glad of a bit of company.' He stammered through the whole
   hour. A nurse rang in afterwards to say it was the best show they had had in months.

   He went back the next week, and the next. With the help of a speech therapist, he
   learned techniques for easing into difficult sounds, and, just as importantly, he
   learned to stop being ashamed of the moments when they did not work. He still
30 stammers occasionally on air. He does not edit it out. 'If I hide it, I'm telling
   every kid who stammers that it's something to hide,' he says. 'I'm not doing that.'

   Letters arrive at the studio every week, many of them from young listeners. One boy
   wrote to say he had answered the register for the first time after hearing Danny
   talk about it. Danny keeps that letter in his wallet. He takes it out to show me,
35 the paper soft from folding. 'That's worth more than any award,' he says.

   As we leave the café, a woman at the next table recognises his voice and asks for a
   photograph. Danny chats to her easily, and when he gets stuck for a moment on the
   word 'pleasure', he simply waits, smiles, and lets the word arrive. She does not
   seem to notice. Neither, I realise, do I.

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *The Cart Race of San Telmo*, by Hannah Wexford, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: The Cart Race of San Telmo
figures.text:
San Telmo clings to the side of its mountain like a cat to a curtain. Its single
   main street drops four hundred metres in a little over a kilometre, twisting back on
   itself seven times between the church at the top and the river at the bottom. On
   three hundred and sixty-four days of the year, the townspeople climb it slowly,
 5 stopping to rest on doorsteps. On the last Sunday in August, they hurl themselves
   down it in home-made wooden carts.

   I had been warned that the race started early, so I arrived at the top just after
   dawn. I need not have hurried. The church clock said seven, but nobody seemed to
   believe it. Teams sat on the steps drinking coffee and arguing about wheels. A man
10 in a helmet decorated with plastic flowers was asleep in his cart. Somebody's
   grandmother was handing out pastries from a basket, and nobody, as far as I could
   tell, was in charge.

   The carts themselves were magnificent. There was a cart shaped like a bathtub, a
   cart shaped like a fish and a cart made almost entirely from an old wardrobe, its
15 doors flapping open like wings. The rules, I was told, are simple. Four wheels. No
   engine. Brakes are recommended. 'Recommended?' I asked. Matteo, the
   eighteen-year-old captain of the wardrobe team, shrugged. 'Some people prefer not
   to,' he said. 'They are usually the winners. Or in hospital.'

   At half past nine, without any announcement I could hear, the first cart simply set
20 off. Then another, and another, at intervals that seemed to depend on nothing but
   courage. The crowd lining the street roared each one on, banging saucepans and
   blowing whistles. I ran to the third bend, where the street narrows between two
   stone walls and turns so sharply that the houses almost touch.

   The fish arrived first, rattling and shrieking, its two riders crouched low and
25 screaming instructions at each other. It hit the bend far too fast, slid sideways in
   a shower of sparks and somehow straightened again, missing the wall by the width of
   a hand. The crowd gasped and then cheered as if a goal had been scored. Behind it
   came the bathtub, which did not straighten, and which ended the race upside down in
   a flower bed, its riders climbing out to bow to tremendous applause.

30 And then the wardrobe. I heard it before I saw it: a deep, wooden thunder bouncing
   off the walls. Matteo and his cousin were wedged inside, their faces white with
   concentration, the doors still flapping. They took the bend on two wheels. For a
   moment the whole thing hung in the air, tilting, and I was sure it was going over.
   Then it crashed back down on all four and vanished round the corner, trailing a long
35 cheer behind it like a banner.

   It won, of course. When I finally reached the bottom of the hill, out of breath and
   slightly deafened, the wardrobe was parked by the river with a garland of flowers on
   its roof, and Matteo was being carried around on the shoulders of his friends. The
   prize, he told me proudly, was a ham, a trophy and the right to start first next
40 year. 'And the hospital?' I asked. He grinned and showed me a bandage on his elbow.
   'Only a little bit,' he said.

   That evening the whole town ate together at long tables in the square, and the
   arguments about wheels began all over again. I asked an old man why San Telmo had
   kept the race going for over sixty years. He thought about it for a long time. 'The
45 rest of the year,' he said, 'the hill wins. One day a year, we win.'

figures.title: Text One: First Week in Tamsa
figures.text:
The bus from the capital took eleven hours, and for the last four of them there was
   nothing outside the window but stones. Not sand, as I had imagined, but stones:
   grey, brown and rust-red, scattered to the horizon as if a giant had emptied out his
   pockets and walked away. Now and then a dust devil spun up from the plain, whirled
 5 for a few seconds like a dancer and collapsed. I pressed my forehead against the
   glass and wondered, not for the first time, what I had done.

   Then, quite suddenly, there was green. Tamsa sits in a fold of the desert where an
   underground river comes close to the surface, and the town has grown along it like a
   necklace of date palms and flat-roofed houses. After so many hours of stone, the
10 colour was almost painful. Children ran beside the bus as it came in, shouting and
   waving. I waved back, and a small boy was so delighted that he tripped over his own
   feet.

   My house belongs to the school. It has two rooms, a courtyard with a single lemon
   tree and a roof where, I was told, everyone sleeps in summer. The walls are made of
15 mud brick, a metre thick, and inside it is wonderfully cool. The furniture consists
   of a bed, a table, two chairs and a large, ancient refrigerator that hums to itself
   all night like an old man remembering a song.

   On my first morning, the headmaster, Mr Haddad, came to collect me. He was a tall,
   careful man who spoke slow, beautiful English and apologised for everything: the
20 heat, the dust, the state of the road, the fact that the school had no photocopier.
   'We have a very good blackboard,' he added, as though offering me a gift. He walked
   me through the market on the way, introducing me to every stallholder by name. By
   the end of the street I had been given four oranges, a bag of dates and an
   invitation to a wedding.

25 The school was a long, low building painted a hopeful shade of blue. My first class
   had forty-one pupils, all of whom stood up when I walked in and said 'Good morning,
   teacher' in perfect unison. I had planned a lively lesson with games and songs.
   Within ten minutes I had abandoned it. They wanted to ask me questions, and they had
   clearly been saving them up for weeks. Did I have a husband? Did it snow in my city?
30 Had I met any famous footballers? Was it true that people in my country kept dogs
   inside their houses?

   I answered as honestly as I could, and they listened with total seriousness,
   occasionally whispering translations to each other. When I admitted that I did not
   know how to cook rice properly, a girl in the front row looked at me with deep pity
35 and promised that her mother would teach me. She did, too, three days later, while
   the rest of the family watched from the doorway and tried very hard not to laugh.

   That first week I made every mistake it was possible to make. I offered my left hand
   to an elderly man. I wore the wrong shoes into a neighbour's house. I got lost in
   the palm groves twice and had to be led home by the same patient goat-herder, who
40 greeted me on the second occasion as if I were an old friend. Each time, people
   forgave me with a smile, a gesture, a cup of sweet tea.

   On the Friday evening I climbed up to my roof and lay on a blanket, watching the
   stars come out. There were more of them than I had ever seen, so many that the dark
   between them seemed crowded. Somewhere below, a radio was playing, and someone was
45 laughing, and the refrigerator hummed its old song. I had come to Tamsa to teach. I
   was beginning to understand that I had a great deal more to learn.

figures.title: Text One: Letting Go
figures.text:
The box arrived on a wet Tuesday in November, carried in by a lorry driver who had
   found it, he said, sitting in the middle of a lay-by 'like it was waiting for a
   bus'. He set it down on the counter very gently, as if it might explode. Inside,
   wrapped in a tea towel printed with lighthouses, was a barn owl.

 5 I had never been so close to one. Its face was a perfect white heart, so smooth it
   looked carved from soap, and in the middle of it two black eyes stared up at me
   without blinking. Its feathers were the colour of toast and honey, freckled with
   tiny grey dots, and it was astonishingly light. When I lifted it, it weighed less
   than a bag of sugar. All that silent menace, I thought, and almost nothing inside.

10 Its left wing hung at a wrong angle. The vet, a brisk woman called Ruth who had seen
   everything twice, felt along the bone with two fingers and pronounced it 'not
   broken, just badly bruised, probably clipped by a car'. It would need four weeks of
   rest and then, if we were lucky, a long period of exercise before it could fly
   again. 'Don't name it,' she said, as she said to every new volunteer. 'It's not
15 yours. It's only borrowing you.'

   I named it anyway, though only in my head. That year had been the worst of my life.
   My mother had been ill since the spring, and every visit to the hospital left me
   feeling emptier and more useless. At the centre, at least, there were things I could
   do. I could chop the chicks into pieces with a pair of scissors. I could clean the
20 cage. I could sit quietly in the corner of the dim shed and watch the owl watching
   me, its head turning slowly through an impossible half-circle, until the world
   shrank to the two of us and the soft patter of rain on the roof.

   By January it was flying the length of the long aviary. The first time it did so I
   was standing at the far end, and it came towards me out of the gloom without a
25 single sound, wings wide, pale as a ghost, and veered away at the last second so
   close that I felt the air move against my cheek. I had read that owls fly silently.
   I had not understood what that meant. It was like being brushed past by a thought.

   Ruth decided it should be released at the end of February, back at the lay-by where
   it had been found, because barn owls do best in the territory they know. I drove out
30 with her at dusk. It was cold and very still, the fields white with frost, the sky
   turning from orange to deep blue above a line of black hedges. I held the box on my
   knees for the whole journey and did not say a word.

   When Ruth opened the door, nothing happened. The owl sat in the dark of the box and
   looked out at the fields, and I began to think it would refuse to go. Then, without
35 any warning, it stepped onto the edge, opened its wings and was gone, gliding low
   over the frost, a pale shape that grew smaller and smaller until I could not tell it
   apart from the mist. I stood with the empty box in my hands for a long time.

   'You did well,' said Ruth, which was the nearest she ever came to praise. I nodded.
   I could not have spoken if I had tried. Driving home, I realised that for the first
40 time in months I was not thinking about the hospital. I was thinking about the owl,
   somewhere out in the cold fields, hunting, free. My mother died in the spring. I
   still go back to the lay-by sometimes at dusk. I have never seen the owl again. I
   have never stopped looking.

   found it, he said, sitting in the middle of a lay-by 'like it was waiting for a

 5 I had never been so close to one. Its face was a perfect white heart, so smooth it
   looked carved from soap, and in the middle of it two black eyes stared up at me
   without blinking. Its feathers were the colour of toast and honey, freckled with
   tiny grey dots, and it was astonishingly light. When I lifted it, it weighed less
   than a bag of sugar. All that silent menace, I thought, and almost nothing inside.

10 Its left wing hung at a wrong angle. The vet, a brisk woman called Ruth who had seen
   everything twice, felt along the bone with two fingers and pronounced it 'not
   broken, just badly bruised, probably clipped by a car'. It would need four weeks of
   rest and then, if we were lucky, a long period of exercise before it could fly
   again. 'Don't name it,' she said, as she said to every new volunteer. 'It's not
15 yours. It's only borrowing you.'

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *The Chess Prize*, by Lin Mei-hua, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: The Chess Prize
figures.text:
My grandfather believed in three things: hard work, cold baths and silence. He had
   been a railway engineer for forty years, and he ran our small flat as if it were a
   timetable. Breakfast was at six fifteen. Homework was checked at seven. Lights went
   out at nine, and if he heard me turning the pages of a book after that, he would
 5 knock once on the wall, very softly, which was worse than any shout.

   He rarely spoke to me except to give instructions. I do not think he disliked me. I
   think he simply did not know what to do with a girl of eleven who had arrived in his
   life with one suitcase after my parents' accident. So he did what he knew. He fed
   me, he paid for my school, and in the evenings he sat by the window with his
10 chessboard, playing against himself, his face as still as a closed door.

   I learned the game by watching. For months I sat across the room pretending to read,
   while in fact I followed every move. I learned how the knight jumps and the bishop
   slides, how a pawn that reaches the far side can become a queen. I never asked him
   to teach me. I was afraid he would say no, and even more afraid he would say yes and
15 find that I was stupid.

   When the school announced a chess tournament, I put my name down without telling
   anyone. I practised in secret on a board I had drawn on the back of a cereal box,
   with buttons for pieces. On the morning of the tournament I told my grandfather I
   was going to the library. He looked at me over his glasses for a long moment and
20 said nothing, which was what he usually said.

   The hall was full of boys. They were older than me, and louder, and most of them had
   real chess sets in wooden boxes. My first opponent laughed when he saw me sit down
   and asked if I was lost. I beat him in twenty-three moves. I beat the second boy,
   and the third. By the afternoon a small crowd had begun to gather around my table,
25 and my hands were shaking so badly that I had to hold the pieces with both fingers
   to stop them falling over.

   I lost the final. I made a careless move with my queen, saw the mistake a second
   after I had let go of the piece, and watched my opponent close in on my king with a
   terrible politeness. I shook his hand and walked to the side of the hall, determined
30 not to cry in front of everyone. That was when I saw him. My grandfather was
   standing at the back, by the fire exit, in his good coat. I had no idea how long he
   had been there.

   We walked home together without speaking. I carried my certificate for second place
   rolled up in my fist, and I was sure he was angry that I had lied about the library.
35 At the door of our building he stopped, and for a moment I thought he was going to
   knock on the wall, the way he did at night. Instead he said, 'Your queen. Move
   seventeen. You were too quick.' Then, after a pause, 'Everything else was correct.'

   It was the longest speech he had ever made to me. That evening, when homework had
   been checked, he did not go to the window. He set the board up on the kitchen table,
40 turned it so that the white pieces faced me, and waited. We played every night after
   that for nine years. He never once let me win. I have never received a prize I
   valued more than those four words: everything else was correct.

figures.title: Text One: The Chess Prize

   been a railway engineer for forty years, and he ran our small flat as if it were a
   timetable. Breakfast was at six fifteen. Homework was checked at seven. Lights went
   out at nine, and if he heard me turning the pages of a book after that, he would
 5 knock once on the wall, very softly, which was worse than any shout.

   think he simply did not know what to do with a girl of eleven who had arrived in his
   life with one suitcase after my parents' accident. So he did what he knew. He fed
   me, he paid for my school, and in the evenings he sat by the window with his
10 chessboard, playing against himself, his face as still as a closed door.

   while in fact I followed every move. I learned how the knight jumps and the bishop
   slides, how a pawn that reaches the far side can become a queen. I never asked him

15 find that I was stupid.

   anyone. I practised in secret on a board I had drawn on the back of a cereal box,

   was going to the library. He looked at me over his glasses for a long moment and
20 said nothing, which was what he usually said.

30 not to cry in front of everyone. That was when I saw him. My grandfather was
   standing at the back, by the fire exit, in his good coat. I had no idea how long he
   had been there.

40 turned it so that the white pieces faced me, and waited. We played every night after

   valued more than those four words: everything else was correct.

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *Whiteout on the Ridge*, by Callum Reid, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: Whiteout on the Ridge
figures.text:
It began, as these things often do, with a beautiful morning. When I left the car
   park at eight o'clock, the sky was a sharp, cloudless blue and the snow on the
   summit glittered like sugar. I had a map, a compass, spare gloves, a flask of soup
   and a forecast that promised a dry day with 'some cloud later'. I remember feeling
 5 slightly smug as I passed a group turning back at the first stile.

   By eleven I was on the ridge, a narrow spine of rock and old snow with steep drops
   on either side. The views were enormous. I could see three lakes, a scattering of
   farms and, far to the west, the grey glint of the sea. I stopped to eat a sandwich
   and take photographs, and it was only when I stood up again that I noticed the
10 cloud.

   It was coming up from the valley on my left, smooth and white, rolling over the edge
   of the ridge like milk boiling over a pan. I had perhaps five minutes before it
   reached me. I spent two of them deciding whether to go on or turn back, and by the
   time I had decided, the decision had been made for me. The world disappeared.

15 A whiteout is very hard to describe to anyone who has not been in one. It is not
   like fog. In fog you can see your own feet. In a whiteout the snow on the ground and
   the cloud in the air become exactly the same colour, and you lose all sense of up
   and down. Within minutes the wind had picked up, driving snow sideways into my face
   so hard that it stung like sand. I could not tell where the ridge ended and the drop
20 began.

   I did what I had been taught and stopped. I crouched down, got out my map and
   compass with fingers that had already gone stiff, and worked out a bearing that
   would take me off the ridge on its gentler, southern side. Then I began to walk,
   counting my paces out loud, stopping every hundred steps to check the needle. My
25 voice sounded thin and strange, as if it belonged to someone else.

   At one point the ground in front of me simply vanished. I stopped with one foot in
   the air, my heart hammering, and lowered myself onto my hands and knees. Ahead,
   where I had been about to step, was nothing but white. I threw a snowball forward
   and did not hear it land. I have no idea how deep that drop was. I have tried very
30 hard not to think about it.

   It took me three hours to come down a slope that would normally take forty minutes.
   When I finally stepped out of the bottom of the cloud, the change was so sudden that
   I almost laughed: green grass, a stone wall, a sheep staring at me with mild
   disapproval. I sat down on the wall and drank the whole flask of soup, which had
35 gone lukewarm, and which was the best thing I have ever tasted.

   I have walked in the mountains for twenty years, and I learned more that day than in
   all the others put together. I learned that a forecast is a guess, not a promise. I
   learned that the group who turned back at the stile were not timid but wise. Most of
   all I learned that the mountain does not care how experienced you are. It only cares
40 whether you are paying attention.

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *Whiteout on the Ridge*, by Callum Reid, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: Whiteout on the Ridge
figures.text:
It began, as these things often do, with a beautiful morning. When I left the car
   park at eight o'clock, the sky was a sharp, cloudless blue and the snow on the
   summit glittered like sugar. I had a map, a compass, spare gloves, a flask of soup
   and a forecast that promised a dry day with 'some cloud later'. I remember feeling
 5 slightly smug as I passed a group turning back at the first stile.

   By eleven I was on the ridge, a narrow spine of rock and old snow with steep drops
   on either side. The views were enormous. I could see three lakes, a scattering of
   farms and, far to the west, the grey glint of the sea. I stopped to eat a sandwich
   and take photographs, and it was only when I stood up again that I noticed the
10 cloud.

   It was coming up from the valley on my left, smooth and white, rolling over the edge
   of the ridge like milk boiling over a pan. I had perhaps five minutes before it
   reached me. I spent two of them deciding whether to go on or turn back, and by the
   time I had decided, the decision had been made for me. The world disappeared.

15 A whiteout is very hard to describe to anyone who has not been in one. It is not
   like fog. In fog you can see your own feet. In a whiteout the snow on the ground and
   the cloud in the air become exactly the same colour, and you lose all sense of up
   and down. Within minutes the wind had picked up, driving snow sideways into my face
   so hard that it stung like sand. I could not tell where the ridge ended and the drop
20 began.

   I did what I had been taught and stopped. I crouched down, got out my map and
   compass with fingers that had already gone stiff, and worked out a bearing that
   would take me off the ridge on its gentler, southern side. Then I began to walk,
   counting my paces out loud, stopping every hundred steps to check the needle. My
25 voice sounded thin and strange, as if it belonged to someone else.

   At one point the ground in front of me simply vanished. I stopped with one foot in
   the air, my heart hammering, and lowered myself onto my hands and knees. Ahead,
   where I had been about to step, was nothing but white. I threw a snowball forward
   and did not hear it land. I have no idea how deep that drop was. I have tried very
30 hard not to think about it.

   It took me three hours to come down a slope that would normally take forty minutes.
   When I finally stepped out of the bottom of the cloud, the change was so sudden that
   I almost laughed: green grass, a stone wall, a sheep staring at me with mild
   disapproval. I sat down on the wall and drank the whole flask of soup, which had
35 gone lukewarm, and which was the best thing I have ever tasted.

   I have walked in the mountains for twenty years, and I learned more that day than in
   all the others put together. I learned that a forecast is a guess, not a promise. I
   learned that the group who turned back at the stile were not timid but wise. Most of
   all I learned that the mountain does not care how experienced you are. It only cares
40 whether you are paying attention.

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *A Morning at the Camel Races*, by Nadia Farouk, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: A Morning at the Camel Races
figures.text:
The race track is a long loop of raked sand on the edge of town, marked out with
   white posts and nothing else. There are no stands. Spectators bring their own
   chairs, or sit on the bonnets of their cars, or simply stand in the soft sand at the
   side of the track with their scarves pulled up against the dust. By six in the
 5 morning, when I arrived, several hundred people were already there, and the air
   smelt of strong coffee, engine oil and camel.

   The camels themselves were waiting in a pen near the start, and they were not what I
   had expected. I had pictured slow, grumpy creatures with drooping lips. These were
   racing camels: tall, slim and long-legged, their coats brushed until they shone like
10 polished wood. Each wore a brightly coloured blanket and a muzzle, and they gazed
   down at the crowd with an expression of enormous superiority, like duchesses at a
   village fair.

   My guide was Khalid, a retired trainer of about seventy who had agreed to explain
   the sport to me. He had owned racing camels for fifty years and spoke about them the
15 way some people speak about their grandchildren. 'That one is lazy,' he said,
   pointing. 'Very talented, but lazy. That one is brave. And that one,' he lowered his
   voice, 'is a genius. But she knows it.'

   Nobody rides the camels any more. Instead, a small robot jockey is strapped to each
   animal's hump, a box of electronics no bigger than a shoebox with a little whip on
20 an arm. The owners control them by radio while driving alongside the track in their
   cars. When I asked Khalid whether he missed the old days, he was quiet for a moment.
   'The camels do not miss them,' he said at last. 'The robots are lighter. And they
   never argue.'

   The start, when it came, was sudden. A rope dropped, and twenty camels burst forward
25 in a great rolling surge of legs and dust, their long necks stretched out, their
   strides so enormous that they seemed to float above the ground. At the same moment
   every car on the road beside the track roared into life. Within seconds, there were
   two races: the camels on the sand and, alongside them, a chaotic convoy of
   four-wheel-drive vehicles, horns blaring, owners leaning out of the windows and
30 shouting instructions into their radios.

   Khalid insisted that we join them. I found myself in the back seat of his nephew's
   car, holding on to the door handle with both hands as we bounced along at sixty
   kilometres an hour, a few metres from the running camels. Dust poured in through the
   open windows. Khalid, in the front, was shouting encouragement at a camel that did
35 not belong to him and had no idea he existed. I have never been so frightened or so
   happy at the same time.

   The genius won. She crossed the line nearly two lengths clear, her robot jockey
   still flicking its tiny whip, and slowed to a dignified walk as if the whole
   business had been slightly beneath her. Her owner, a young man in mirrored
40 sunglasses, leapt from his car and danced in the sand. Several people hugged Khalid,
   although he had nothing to do with it.

   Afterwards, over more coffee, I asked him what he loved most about the races. I
   expected him to talk about speed, or money, or the thrill of winning. Instead he
   looked out at the camels, who were being led back to their pens, blankets steaming
45 in the rising heat. 'My grandfather raced camels,' he said. 'And his grandfather.
   The cars are new. The robots are new. But the camels are the same. When I watch them
   run, I am watching my family.'

intro: The following question is based on Text One, *A Morning at the Camel Races*, by Nadia Farouk, in the Insert.

figures.title: Text One: A Morning at the Camel Races
figures.text:
The race track is a long loop of raked sand on the edge of town, marked out with
   white posts and nothing else. There are no stands. Spectators bring their own
   chairs, or sit on the bonnets of their cars, or simply stand in the soft sand at the
   side of the track with their scarves pulled up against the dust. By six in the
 5 morning, when I arrived, several hundred people were already there, and the air
   smelt of strong coffee, engine oil and camel.

   The camels themselves were waiting in a pen near the start, and they were not what I
   had expected. I had pictured slow, grumpy creatures with drooping lips. These were
   racing camels: tall, slim and long-legged, their coats brushed until they shone like
10 polished wood. Each wore a brightly coloured blanket and a muzzle, and they gazed
   down at the crowd with an expression of enormous superiority, like duchesses at a
   village fair.

   My guide was Khalid, a retired trainer of about seventy who had agreed to explain
   the sport to me. He had owned racing camels for fifty years and spoke about them the
15 way some people speak about their grandchildren. 'That one is lazy,' he said,
   pointing. 'Very talented, but lazy. That one is brave. And that one,' he lowered his
   voice, 'is a genius. But she knows it.'

   Nobody rides the camels any more. Instead, a small robot jockey is strapped to each
   animal's hump, a box of electronics no bigger than a shoebox with a little whip on
20 an arm. The owners control them by radio while driving alongside the track in their
   cars. When I asked Khalid whether he missed the old days, he was quiet for a moment.
   'The camels do not miss them,' he said at last. 'The robots are lighter. And they
   never argue.'

   The start, when it came, was sudden. A rope dropped, and twenty camels burst forward
25 in a great rolling surge of legs and dust, their long necks stretched out, their
   strides so enormous that they seemed to float above the ground. At the same moment
   every car on the road beside the track roared into life. Within seconds, there were
   two races: the camels on the sand and, alongside them, a chaotic convoy of
   four-wheel-drive vehicles, horns blaring, owners leaning out of the windows and
30 shouting instructions into their radios.

   Khalid insisted that we join them. I found myself in the back seat of his nephew's
   car, holding on to the door handle with both hands as we bounced along at sixty
   kilometres an hour, a few metres from the running camels. Dust poured in through the
   open windows. Khalid, in the front, was shouting encouragement at a camel that did
35 not belong to him and had no idea he existed. I have never been so frightened or so
   happy at the same time.

   The genius won. She crossed the line nearly two lengths clear, her robot jockey
   still flicking its tiny whip, and slowed to a dignified walk as if the whole
   business had been slightly beneath her. Her owner, a young man in mirrored
40 sunglasses, leapt from his car and danced in the sand. Several people hugged Khalid,
   although he had nothing to do with it.

   Afterwards, over more coffee, I asked him what he loved most about the races. I
   expected him to talk about speed, or money, or the thrill of winning. Instead he
   looked out at the camels, who were being led back to their pens, blankets steaming
45 in the rising heat. 'My grandfather raced camels,' he said. 'And his grandfather.
   The cars are new. The robots are new. But the camels are the same. When I watch them
   run, I am watching my family.'
